The Best Christmas Tree Varieties: 8 Types Compared

by Farmers' Almanac Staff Updated: November 22, 2026
EmailFacebookPinterestX
Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 7:22
Instaread

The best real Christmas tree depends on what you want most. Choose a Balsam fir for its classic fragrance, a Fraser fir for a well-rounded tree with good needle retention, or a Noble fir or Scotch pine for sturdy branches and ornaments. If you like soft needles, consider a Douglas fir; for blue-gray color, look at a Colorado blue spruce.

A tree’s variety matters, but so do its freshness, when it was cut, and how well it is watered. No species comes with a guaranteed number of weeks indoors. Here’s how eight popular Christmas tree varieties compare.

Christmas tree varieties at a glance

8 popular Christmas tree types

1. Balsam fir

Balsam fir is prized for its familiar, resinous fragrance. It has dark-green needles, an attractive shape and a scent that can linger through the holiday season. It’s a good choice if the smell of a fresh tree is part of what makes Christmas feel like Christmas.

2. Fraser fir

Fraser fir is a popular all-around choice. Its dark blue-green needles, pleasant scent and upward-turning branches give it a compact, balanced shape. It is also known for good needle retention, though the tree still needs consistent watering.

3. Douglas fir

Douglas fir has soft needles that radiate around the branches. When crushed, they give off a sweet fragrance. Its full appearance makes it a familiar choice for homes that want a classic, well-filled tree.

4. Scotch pine (Scots pine)

Scotch pine is known for excellent needle retention and stiff branches that work well with decorations. Its needles can remain attached even as the tree dries, but that does not mean a dry tree should stay indoors. Check it regularly and take it down when it becomes very dry.

5. Noble fir

Noble fir has blue-green needles that turn upward, showing more of the branches beneath. Its stiff branches and long keepability make it a strong option for heavier ornaments. The boughs are also often used for wreaths and garlands.

6. Colorado blue spruce

Colorado blue spruce stands out for its blue-gray foliage and symmetrical shape. It has good needle retention, but its needles are sharp, so take care when handling or decorating it.

7. Concolor fir (white fir)

Also called white fir, concolor fir has a pleasing shape, good needle retention and a noticeable aroma. Its foliage can range from blue-green to green, offering a different look from the darker, traditional firs.

8. White pine

White pine has long, soft, flexible needles and a more open look than many densely shaped trees. It has little fragrance and is not the best choice for heavy ornaments, but it may suit families who prefer a lighter, less crowded silhouette.

Regional Christmas tree varieties

The trees you see at local lots often reflect what growers raise nearby. Douglas fir is a major Christmas tree in the Pacific Northwest, while Fraser fir is widely grown in North Carolina. In the Southeast, shoppers may also find Leyland cypress or Virginia pine. Norway spruce is another familiar option, especially in the Northeast, but it can lose needles quickly if it was cut too early or allowed to dry out.

Ask the grower or lot which varieties are freshest and perform well in your area. The National Christmas Tree Association’s variety guide has more details about tree characteristics.

Which Christmas tree holds its needles the longest?

Fraser fir, Balsam fir, Noble fir and Scotch pine are all known for good needle retention. Colorado blue spruce also retains needles well when it is cared for. But the species alone won’t tell you exactly how long a tree will look fresh: the tree’s condition when you buy it and whether its stand stays filled with water matter, too. The NCTA recommends checking a tree’s freshness before you bring it home and keeping water above the base of the trunk.

How to choose a fresh Christmas tree

Before you shop, measure both the height and width of the space where the tree will stand. Remember to leave room for the stand and topper.

At the lot, check the tree’s condition:

  • Gently run a branch through your hand. Green outer needles should not fall off easily.
  • Bend an outer branch. It should be pliable, not brittle.
  • Look for healthy color and avoid trees with a musty smell or excessive needle loss.
  • A few older, brown needles near the trunk can be normal; widespread loss of green outer needles is a warning sign.

For more help, see our guide on how to pick a Christmas tree.

How to keep a real Christmas tree fresh

When you get the tree home, cut about half an inch from the bottom of the trunk and place it in water as soon as you can. Use a stand with enough capacity for the tree, and check the water level every day so the cut end stays submerged. Plain tap water is best; additives are not needed.

Keep the tree away from fireplaces, heaters, heat vents and direct sunlight to slow drying. For advice on timing your purchase and setup, read when to put up your Christmas tree. When the tree becomes very dry, take it down.

Frequently asked questions

What is the most fragrant Christmas tree?

Balsam fir is known for retaining its familiar Christmas-tree fragrance. Douglas fir has a sweet scent when its needles are crushed. Fragrance is subjective, so if scent matters to you, compare varieties at the lot before choosing.

Which Christmas tree is best for heavy ornaments?

Noble fir and Scotch pine are known for stiff branches that support heavier ornaments. Fraser fir is another popular choice for its sturdy, upward-turning branches.

Is a Norway spruce a good Christmas tree?

It can be, especially if you find a fresh tree and keep it watered. Norway spruce is known for poor needle retention if it dries out, so check its condition carefully before buying.

How long will a real Christmas tree last indoors?

There isn’t a guaranteed number of weeks. Freshness, the time since cutting, indoor heat and steady watering all affect how long a tree stays in good condition.

Should I add anything to the tree’s water?

No. Plain tap water is best. Keep the reservoir filled so the base of the trunk remains submerged.

Which Christmas tree variety do you bring home each year? Tell us in the comments.
